kurz: Why a loss of €1,000 weighs roughly twice as heavily as a gain of €1,000, what this means for your portfolio and what German tax law has to say about it.

bloecke.md:
Two portfolios stand at €80,000 today. One has risen from €60,000, the other has fallen from €100,000. Before tax, both are worth the same, because they contain the same securities with the same prospects. For tax purposes, the second portfolio has the advantage, because after a sale its paper loss can be offset against gains, whereas the paper gain of the first incurs tax on sale. Nevertheless, you perceive the first portfolio as a success and the second as a painful loss.

Classical decision theory does not take this difference into account. It assumes that people evaluate their final wealth. In 1979, in the journal *Econometrica*, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that this is not true empirically. What is evaluated is the change relative to a **reference point**. On the stock exchange, this is almost always your own purchase price. This figure comes from the past, no other market participant knows it, and it has no influence whatsoever on future price movements.

## Properties of the value function

[[Prospect theory]] describes the evaluation of outcomes using a function with three features. First, it passes through the reference point and not through the zero point of wealth. Second, it is curved in both directions. The difference between €0 and €500 of gain feels larger than that between €4,500 and €5,000, although it is €500 both times. This property is called diminishing sensitivity. Third, the loss branch is much steeper than the gain branch. For investors, this third property has the most expensive consequences.

bloecke.erklaerung: The usual parameterisation of the value function. The exponent 0.88 produces the curvature, and the factor in front of the loss branch captures loss aversion. Both branches are equally curved; the loss branch is merely stretched.
variablen: Gain or loss relative to the reference point, not final wealth
Curvature of both branches, typical estimate from Tversky/Kahneman (1992)
Loss aversion factor lambda from the meta-analysis by Brown et al. (2024)
bloecke.beispiel: A gain of €1,000 brings 437 units of value, while a loss of €1,000 costs 853 units of value. To offset a loss of €1,000 emotionally, a gain of around €2,100 is needed.

bloecke.titel: Perceived value of gains and losses
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with the usual parameters (exponent 0.88, loss factor 1.955). The dashed straight line shows a valuation that weights gains and losses equally; the left branch of the curve lies well below it.

serien.name: Equal weighting of pleasure and pain

bloecke.md: The frequently quoted value lambda = 2.25 comes from Tversky/Kahneman (1992). The most reliable figure comes from the meta-analysis by Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer (2024, *Journal of Economic Literature*), which evaluates 607 estimates from 150 studies. It arrives at lambda = 1.955 with a 95% interval of 1.82 to 2.10. The rule of thumb that losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as gains of the same size is therefore well supported, whereas precision to the second decimal place is not.

## Weighting of probabilities

The value function describes how outcomes are evaluated. The second building block of the theory describes how their probabilities enter into the evaluation, and they do so non-linearly. Small probabilities are overweighted, medium and large ones underweighted. A 1% chance feels like five, and the jump from 95% to 100% weighs more heavily than the one from 60% to 65%. The exact parameters of this weighting function are less well established empirically than the loss factor, but its direction is well documented.

Together, the two building blocks give rise to the **fourfold pattern of risk attitudes**. It explains why the same person buys lottery tickets and takes out insurance, locks in paper gains quickly and sits out paper losses for years. These behaviours do not contradict each other, because all four follow from the same valuation rules.

bloecke.unter: Whether someone acts in a risk-averse or risk-seeking way depends on the sign of the outcome and the size of the probability, not on character.
bloecke.yLabel: gain at top, loss at bottom

felder.text: Small chances of winning are overweighted. Turbo certificates, warrants far out of the money, the one share that is supposed to make up for everything.
The probable but uncertain gain is exchanged for the smaller certain one. The paper gain is taken before anything else can happen.
A premium is willingly paid for the small probability of a large loss. Sensible for existential risks, expensive for mobile phones and luggage.
The probable loss is exchanged for the small chance of breaking even after all. This is where the disposition effect arises.

bloecke.md:
## The disposition effect

Hersh Shefrin and Meir Statman gave the pattern its name in 1985. It states that investors sell winners too early and hold on to losers too long. In 1998 Terrance Odean measured it using around 10,000 accounts at a US discount broker for the years 1987 to 1993. He compared rates rather than absolute numbers, because investors with many winners in their portfolio inevitably also sell more winners.

Of all positions that were in profit on a trading day with a sale, 14.8% were realised; of the positions at a loss, only 9.8%. Winners were therefore sold around one and a half times as often as losers. The t-statistic of -35 shows that this difference is not due to chance.

In December the pattern reverses. Then 12.8% of losers are realised and only 10.8% of winners, because losses can be offset for tax purposes at the end of the year. So investors are able to realise losses, but do not do so in the other eleven months.

bloecke.titel: Realisation rates over the year and in December
bloecke.unter: Odean (1998), around 10,000 accounts, 1987 to 1993. The chart shows the proportion of positions in profit or at a loss, respectively, that were sold on a day with a sale.

bloecke.titel: The cost of sitting it out
bloecke.md:
Odean tracked how both groups performed afterwards. Over the following 252 trading days, the winners that had been sold achieved on average an excess return over the market index that was 3.4 percentage points higher than that of the losers that had been held. The assumption “it has already fallen so far, now it has to come back” was therefore not borne out on average; in fact, the opposite happened.

An investor who has €30,000 tied up in positions held only because of their purchase price loses, at this order of magnitude, around €1,020 a year. The loss arises anew each time, because the mistake is repeated with every single decision. The amount is an average across thousands of accounts and not a forecast for any individual share.

## Tax consequences in Germany

In Germany, tax favours the opposite of what the [[Disposition effect|disposition effect]] brings about. Selling a winner immediately triggers 25% [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge, a total of 26.375% (Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), withheld by the bank under Section 43a EStG). To the extent that the [[Saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)]] of €1,000 (€2,000 for joint assessment, Section 20(9) EStG) has been used up, this money flows out immediately and is no longer available for investment. As long as a gain exists only on paper, the tax on it is deferred. The sale ends this deferral.

Selling a loser, by contrast, creates a loss that can be used for tax purposes. It is recorded in the bank's [[Loss offset pot (Verlustverrechnungstopf)|loss offset pot (Verlustverrechnungstopf)]] and, if it cannot be offset in the current year, carried forward indefinitely (Section 20(6) sentences 1 to 3 EStG).

bloecke.titel: Limits of the share loss pot
bloecke.md:
Losses from selling individual shares may only be offset against gains from selling individual shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). Dividends, interest, bonds, certificates and ETF gains do not count; they go through the general loss pot. An investor who sells a share at a loss and afterwards only saves into ETFs therefore collects losses in a pot for which no matching gains arise any more.

In addition, losses at bank A are not automatically offset against gains at bank B. This requires a loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung) under Section 43a(3) sentences 4 and 5 EStG, which must be applied for by 15 December of the current year. The application is irrevocable, and the deadline cannot be extended.

## Evaluation frequency and loss aversion

Loss aversion only has an effect when a loss becomes visible. Whether that happens depends almost entirely on how short the periods under consideration are. In 1995 Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler called this **myopic loss aversion** (myopic means short-sighted). Loss aversion combined with a short evaluation period explains why equities have historically had to pay such a high risk premium. The premium compensates investors for having to endure losses that are visible every day.

Behind this lies a simple probability calculation. With an expected return of 7% a year and a [[Volatility|volatility]] of 18%, the outcome in the short term is determined almost entirely by chance. Only over years does the expected value become more important than the dispersion. An investor who looks at the portfolio every day is therefore practically watching a coin toss. If the result is negative, they give it double weight.

bloecke.titel: Share of negative periods by length of period considered
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a normal distribution, 7% expected annual return and 18% dispersion, excluding costs and taxes. The return is the same in all cases; all that changes is how often losses are visible.

bloecke.md: The Deutsches Aktieninstitut (German Equity Institute) runs the same calculation with actual DAX prices. Across all 20-year periods of the past 50 years, the return was between 3.3% and 15.2% a year, 8.4% on average. Not a single one of these periods was negative. In the worst single year (2002), the same index lost 43.9%. The same prices therefore paint a very different picture depending on the length of the period considered. Calculated excluding costs and taxes, as of 31 December 2025.

## Consequences for stop rules

A selling rule does not predict prices. Its benefit comes from the point in time at which it is set. When you buy, you are neutral towards the position. There is no reference point and no paper loss yet, and your own prestige is not yet tied to it. At this point you can decide what would refute the investment thesis and what happens then. After a loss, this decision is no longer possible, because you are then in the risk-seeking quadrant and every rule looks like excessive caution.

A written rule is therefore worth more than an order. It does not have to name a price. The rule “I will sell if the investment thesis is refuted” is more precise than any percentage threshold, provided the thesis was written down in one sentence at the time of purchase.

A [[Stop-loss order|stop-loss order]] is not insurance against losses. As soon as the threshold is touched, it becomes a market order and is executed at the next tradable price. In the event of an overnight price gap, this price can be far below the threshold. A stop-limit order limits this deviation but in return may not be executed at all, precisely when it would matter.

For a broadly diversified world portfolio, such a rule makes no sense anyway. It turns a temporary market movement into a realised loss and then raises the question of when to get back in. Nobody can answer this question. Stop rules belong, if anywhere, with individual speculative positions of limited size and not with the core holdings of your wealth.

bloecke.titel: Portfolio maintenance without a reference point
bloecke.md:
- A different reference point helps. Instead of “Am I in profit on this position?”, the question then becomes “Does its weighting still match the target portfolio?” Showing the purchase price in the portfolio view is a design decision by the bank. The purchase price says nothing about the position's prospects; it only determines the taxable gain on sale.
- The repurchase test asks: “Would I buy this position again today at this price if I had its value in cash?” If the answer is no and the position is held anyway, that is solely down to the purchase price.
- [[Rebalancing]] within fixed ranges buys, according to rules, what has fallen and sells what has risen. This is the exact reverse of the disposition effect, without any decision having to be made at the moment of the loss.
- A lower evaluation frequency, meaning price push notifications switched off and fixed dates, is the most effective known countermeasure and has nothing to do with laziness.
- Tax questions get their own date. The loss pots are checked at the beginning of December, with an eye on Section 20(6) EStG and the certificate deadline, and on no other occasion.

To get back to the purchase price after a loss, a larger percentage rise is needed than the percentage lost, because the rise starts from a smaller base:

- After minus 20%, plus 25% is needed.
- After minus 30%, plus 42.9% is needed.
- After minus 50%, plus 100% is needed.
- After minus 70%, plus 233% is needed.

More important than this asymmetry is a confusion. For the gain needed, it makes no difference which share delivers it. The 42.9% can come from the position that has fallen or from any other investment into which the remaining capital flows after the sale. The purchase price links the two questions, although they have nothing to do with each other.

bloecke.text: At the stock exchange, two times two is never four, but five minus one.

bloecke.md: Kostolany's patience formula describes the same situation without any mathematical derivation. The expected result does arrive, but an interim loss has to be endured first. Investors who lack the nerve for this have, in his description, “shaky hands” and sell at the wrong moment. Research differs from this only in that it can put a figure on what these shaky hands cost.

mitnehmen: What is evaluated is the change relative to a reference point, not the account balance; on the stock exchange this is usually your own purchase price, a figure with no predictive power at all.
Losses weigh about twice as heavily as gains of the same size; the most reliable estimate puts the factor at around 1.96.

The disposition effect arises in the risk-seeking loss quadrant; Odean measures 14.8% of gains realised against 9.8% of losses realised, and the losers that were held lagged behind by 3.4 percentage points in the following year.

German tax law favours the opposite, because selling at a gain immediately costs 26.375%, while selling at a loss creates a loss that can be carried forward, although for individual shares it can only be offset against share gains (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG).
Fixed precautions work better than insight, namely looking at the portfolio less often, setting selling rules at the time of purchase and rebalancing within ranges.

begriffe.text: The benchmark against which an outcome is perceived as a gain or a loss. On the stock exchange this is usually your own purchase price, less often the all-time high or a target value, but never final wealth itself.

The central building block of prospect theory, an S-shaped valuation curve through the reference point. It flattens out in both directions and is around twice as steep in the loss range as in the gain range.

The observation that a loss weighs roughly twice as heavily as a gain of the same size. The factor estimated by meta-analysis is 1.955 (Brown et al. 2024). Loss aversion should not be confused with risk aversion, which relates to fluctuations and not to a reference point.

Loss aversion combined with short evaluation periods. The more often a portfolio is looked at, the more often losses are visible and the more risk-averse the decisions become, even though the return remains unchanged.

A separately kept offsetting pot at the bank for losses from selling individual shares. Under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG, these losses may only be offset against gains from share sales, not against ETF gains, interest or dividends.
